name: Ridgeline
basis: stacked hidden-line plot lifted by brightness (how)

lumenary.blurb: The picture drawn as a stack of lines, each one lifted wherever the picture is bright, like the pulsar plot on a famous album sleeve. Every ridge hides the ones behind it, so the face rises out of the dark in a single unbroken contour at a time.

facts.era: The pulsar plot of 1970; the album sleeve of 1979
facts.bestOn: Pictures with a bright subject on a dark or plain ground

why: A stack of lines, each lifted where the picture is bright, gives the strongest sense of a hill from the least ink. Because every line hides those behind it, the eye does the rest: it reads the bumps as a surface with a light on it, and fills in the face. It is about the cheapest way to draw a shape, and it is why the pulsar plot looked like a mountain range.
how: Blur the picture so that a ridge follows shapes and not noise.
Space horizontal baselines evenly down the picture.
Lift each baseline, point by point, by the brightness of the picture beneath it.
Fill below each line with the background colour, so that it hides the lines behind it.
Stroke the line, with a soft glow, in white, amber, green or the picture’s own colours.
history: In 1967 Jocelyn Bell Burnell found the first pulsars, and in 1970 the astronomer Harold Craft plotted successive pulses of the pulsar CP 1919 as stacked lines, each hiding those behind it. The picture appeared in the Cambridge Encyclopaedia of Astronomy (1977), and in 1979 the designer Peter Saville used it, as white on black, for Joy Division’s album Unknown Pleasures. It has been copied ever since. The method itself, a hidden-line plot, goes back to the first computer graphics of the 1960s.
terms: Drawing a 3D shape so that lines behind a nearer surface are not shown.
The flat line a ridge would lie on if the picture beneath it were completely dark.
A line made of many short straight segments joined end to end.
paragraphs: With n lines, the spacing is d = (H - 2m) / (n + a), where m is the margin (5% of the width) and a is the height of the ridges in line spacings (0.5 to 9). Line i has its baseline at y_i = m + a d + i/(n - 1) (H - 2m - a d). Along the line, at columns whose spacing shrinks as the detail slider rises, the point is lifted by a d b^1.12, where b is the brightness of the picture beneath it after two box blurs of radius 0.42 d (or 1 - b if the ridges should rise where the picture is dark). Lines further back are drawn narrower by the factor lerp(1 - 0.42 P, 1, i/(n - 1)), with P the perspective slider.

The lines are drawn from the back, the top, to the front. Each one is first filled down to the bottom of the picture with the background colour, which is the whole of the hidden-line removal: anything drawn earlier, and now lower on the page, disappears. The line is then stroked, with a wider, fainter copy beneath it for the glow. For the picture’s own colours the stroke is a horizontal gradient whose stops are the blurred colour of the picture at the line’s row, brightened until the strongest channel reaches 255.

equations.note: The height of line i: b is the blurred brightness, a the ridge height in line spacings and n the number of lines.
Perspective: lines further back are drawn narrower about the centre c_x.

dials.label: Ridges rise where the picture is

presets.text: Fewer, taller ridges on black look like the original pulsar plot.
Black ink on paper with the hidden lines left showing gives an engraved look.
The picture’s own colours with some perspective make a glowing landscape.
